title: Mountains to Atolls
description: A schematic elevation staircase from a Maldives coral atoll across the Indian Ocean, through Nepal's Terai, Kathmandu and Bhutan's capital Thimphu, to Mount Everest (8,848.86 m). A sea-level slider (0 to 2 m) shows that a rise invisible at mountain scale floods a large share of a sample low atoll island, with the IPCC AR6 likely 2100 ranges shaded.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: South Asian cultures
Geography
Nepal
Bhutan
Maldives
Sea-level rise
publisher: Roots & Rivers: An Interactive Guide to South Asian Cultures for High School Students
audience: Students, Educators, South Asian student club leaders
learningObjectives: Compare the elevations of the Maldives, the Terai, Kathmandu, Thimphu and Mount Everest on one schematic profile.
Explain why a sea-level rise of under a meter is invisible at mountain scale but serious for low atoll islands.
Relate the IPCC's likely sea-level rise ranges for 2100 to the height of Maldivian islands.
prerequisites: Reading a graph with a labeled vertical axis in meters
Knowing where the Himalaya and the Indian Ocean are (Chapter 1)
keyQuestions: How many times higher is Mount Everest than the Maldives' highest natural ground?
Why does a 1 m sea-level rise barely show on the mountain panel?
How much of a low atoll island could lie below sea level under the IPCC's 2100 ranges?
misconceptions: A sea-level rise of under a meter is too small to matter.
The Maldives is just a resort, not a country where people live.
Mountain countries face no climate risk from warming.
controls: Click or tap a place marker
